news.title: 《文明》《幽浮》开发工作室Firaxis Games裁员三分之一
news.summary_raw: Take-Two （R星及2K的母公司）旗下负责开发《文明》《幽浮》的游戏工作室 Firaxis Games 于日前宣布裁员约60人，占员工总数的三分之一左右。2K Games 发言人随后证实，工作室负责人 Heather Hazen 也将离职。 2K Games发言人在声明中表示，Firaxis 正在进行重组并重新聚焦核心优势，继续开发在过去30年里树立行业标准的策略游戏。根据发言人的说法，作为调整的一部分，工作室正在缩减规模，以专注于设计、技术和玩家体验。虽然这一决定相当艰难，但对开启Firaxis的下一阶段至关重要。 Firaxis去年推出的最新作品《文明7》市场反响褒贬不一，但此后陆续获得了大量更新。据未获授权公开发言的知情人士透露，Firaxis一直在开发一款新的《幽浮》游戏。不过这款游戏的开发过程并不顺利，今年夏天还错过了一个重要节点。知情人士表示，新《幽浮》项目的开发仍会继续，但此次裁员可能会给项目带来较大变动。

2K Games发言人在声明中表示，Firaxis 正在进行重组并重新聚焦核心优势，继续开发在过去30年里树立行业标准的策略游戏。根据发言人的说法，作为调整的一部分，工作室正在缩减规模，以专注于设计、技术和玩家体验。虽然这一决定相当艰难，但对开启Firaxis的下一阶段至关重要。
Firaxis去年推出的最新作品《文明7》市场反响褒贬不一，但此后陆续获得了大量更新。据未获授权公开发言的知情人士透露，Firaxis一直在开发一款新的《幽浮》游戏。不过这款游戏的开发过程并不顺利，今年夏天还错过了一个重要节点。知情人士表示，新《幽浮》项目的开发仍会继续，但此次裁员可能会给项目带来较大变动。

members.title: 5亿做研发、1亿建生态，B站旗舰新作想重塑三国SLG规则
B站新作定档平安夜：SLG赛道凭什么需要“王道”

news.body:
国内SLG赛道，已经很久没有迎来这样一位重量级的挑战者了。
11月14日，在广州地标广州塔举办的线下定档品鉴会上，由光荣特库摩《三国志》系列正版授权、哔哩哔哩游戏发行的沙盘策略旗舰新作《三国志：王道天下》（以下简称《三王》），正式宣布将于12月24日开启全平台公测。
从品鉴会释放的信息来看，无论是研发底盘还是发行资源，B站都在这个项目上拿出了罕见的重投入规格。
在研发侧，成都奇侠互娱历经五年研发，三次大版本美术迭代，精心雕琢，把项目预算拉高至5亿元，团队研发人力规模更是达到国内主流同类项目的1.5倍。厚积之下，项目组在公测前便一口气完成了前三个赛季、足以支撑超半年运营的完整内容储备，这种高规格的工业化管线在近几年的SLG新品中颇为少见。发布会当晚，曾投出多款现象级大作、同时也是奇侠互娱投资方的英雄游戏CEO吴旦亦亲临现场，为各大玩家同盟授旗，尽显资本与行业对产品品质的笃定。
在发行动作上，官方邀请实力派影帝段奕宏出任品牌代言人，其一贯沉稳的银幕质感，恰好为这款新作定下了“重思战场章法”的成熟策略基调，B站更在现场宣布首年投入不低于1亿元现金及超1亿元价值的抖音+B站流量扶持，用于创作者与同盟生态建设。
熟悉SLG市场的人都清楚，这并不是B站第一次在这个赛道上亮剑。
两年前，《三国：谋定天下》（以下简称《三谋》）曾凭借差异化打法，在高度固化的三国SLG市场撕开了一道口子，创下B站游戏史上最快突破10亿元流水的纪录。时至今日，国内SLG早已迈入典型的存量博弈深水区，大盘增速放缓、头部产品凭借深厚的同盟社交资产筑起高墙，后来者若想单纯靠微创新或复制过往成功路径，突围难度已成倍增加。
正因如此，行业对B站第二款SLG的落子格外关注，显然，B站并没有打算简单复刻《三谋》的经验，从《三国志》系列正版授权到重塑战场策略，《三王》正在书写新的历史。
玩法破局
在过去十余年里，市面上三国题材SLG的战斗核心，实际上大多在反复演算同一道题。
无论是早期的纯战法技能联动，还是近几年流行的阵型排布，传统SLG的配队逻辑始终局限于“武将加战法”的二维数值框体之内。早期武将池尚浅时，玩家还能摸索出百花齐放的套路；可随着赛季不断更迭，新卡与新战法越出越多，真正能上场抗衡的主流阵容却越收越窄。
一旦某几套组合在数值效率上跑出优势，便会迅速固化为垄断环境的“版本唯一解”。玩家倾向于按图索骥照抄作业、追逐新卡、拉满红度，最初钻研策略的乐趣也在一轮轮数值膨胀中逐渐消磨。
发布会上，哔哩哔哩游戏发行负责人宋词在复盘品类痛点时提出了一个核心诉求：必须把策略重新推回每一场交锋的中心位置。
而《三王》给出的破局思路相当干脆——在武将与战法之外引入“沙盘空间”作为第三维变量，将延续十余年的二维数值对撞，升维至真实的“三维战场”空间博弈。
它并非简单套上一层战棋玩法的外壳，战棋虽然战术维度丰富，但单局耗时久、手动操作繁琐，塞进强调大地图实时对抗的SLG里，其间的平衡度不好把控。
《三王》在设计上对这个“度”的拿捏相当克制：交战全程采用纯自动演算且默认跳过动画（支持随时回看完整战报），玩家的所有策略重心依然聚焦在最熟悉的战前配将与布阵环节，既守住了SLG原有的明快节奏，又让胜负脱离了数值碾压。
在这个微型沙盘内，游戏叠加了前后排站位、部队移速、攻击射程、地格属性、召唤物以及移动阻挡等全新规则，它们均可与武将技能产生化学反应。这意味着，战场空间本身成了左右战局的关键因子——即便使用完全相同的一组武将，只要站位与战场环境有变，最终打出的结果也可能截然不同。
品鉴会现场演示的几组案例，清晰勾勒出了这套空间机制下的克制闭环：
比如依赖射程与卡位制造天然“嘲讽”：在过往的SLG中，前排肉盾想要掩护后排，往往需要用到珍贵的战法格去携带嘲讽技能，而在《三王》里，由于引入了真实的移动步数与射程判定，敌方部队会优先攻击步入射程的眼前单位。玩家只需巧妙排布前后排次序，把吕蒙顶在阵前，就能迫使高爆发的吕布停下冲锋脚步优先清理前排，不耗费战法格便自然形成了火力牵制。
比如凭移速与空间实现“绕后切C”：面对正面厚重的抗伤防线，机动性极强的赵云则可依托高移速与自带技能，在沙盘格子间连续腾挪穿插，绕过前排盾兵直扑敌军后排脆皮输出，打出类似“侧翼环绕”的奇袭效果。
比如用召唤与阻挡反制高机动流：面对赵云这类高移速骑兵的穿插，游戏也有不少应对之法，如张角唤出的黄巾兵卒、袁绍架设的防御箭塔会实打实占据地格并产生碰撞，直接封死骑兵的迂回通道。
从位移、射程与沙盘的配合，到召唤物的走位封锁，《三王》整套战斗底层形成了一环扣一环的动态制约。
更值得关注的是，研发团队并未把这套三维空间做成一锤子买卖的玩法噱头，而是为其铺设了一条以“战场规则演变”取代“数值堆砌”的长线赛季路线：
按照现场公开的研发规划，S1赛季将完整落地基础三维规则与2000×2000经典大沙盘，帮助玩家平稳建立空间博弈的直觉；迈入S2赛季后，沙盘内将增设“伤害蔓延”与“强制位移”等进阶机制，部队站位不再开局定死，技能交互将碰撞出更多动态变数；
而到了S3赛季，局内微缩棋盘将与大地图沙盘深度打通——大地图上的泥沼、荆棘等特殊地貌会真实同步到战斗棋盘之中。届时，同一个赵云在开阔平原上尚可策马七进七出，一旦踏入泥泞沼泽或狭窄关隘，移速与输出便会遭受地形掣肘，甚至反被远程队伍“放风筝”。
当战场规则与地形风貌每个赛季都在动态刷新，所谓的“最强阵容”便只存在于特定环境之下。老武将不会因为新卡推出就沦为仓库废纸，反而总能在新的地形规则下重获高光，这从机制源头上遏制了SLG玩家深恶痛绝的“撕卡”痛点。
当然，战斗变量的增多势必会抬高玩家的试错成本。为了在“策略纵深”与“上手门槛”之间取得平衡，《三王》在减负与长草期体验上同样下足了功夫。
一方面，游戏实装了自动铺路、自动预约攻城以及工程队系统，近期三测中还砍掉了繁琐的兵种研究、支持一键无损更替战法；针对三维空间带来的战果不确定性，游戏内置了“战前AI战局推演”功能，协助时间有限的玩家在开荒期提前预判胜负、压低战损。
另一方面，为了填补赛季中后期的长草期空虚，游戏推出了无需练度、实时公平轮抽BP的1V1竞技“风云演武”，以及支持离线自动连战的“烽火会战”和融合皮影戏美学的“舌战”玩法，让热衷钻研配将的硬核考究党与追求轻松体验的休闲玩家，都能在同盟大战之外找到各自的乐趣落点。
商业化破局
《三王》这些精妙的三维战场，想要在玩家的研究碰撞下完全发挥出预期效果，依赖于一个前提：相对完整的配将阵容。如果连基础的配将阵容都凑不齐，再深邃的策略博弈最终也只能沦为少数人的自娱自乐。
过去两年，“价格战”几乎成了新晋SLG突围的标配，单抽降价、福利翻倍屡见不鲜。但在品鉴会现场，《三王》展现出的商业化思路走得更远：游戏直接取消传统渠道服，将原本属于渠道分成的利润让渡出来，转化为面向全体玩家的“终身免费月卡”。
每天上线即可白拿80黄金，永久有效、无需续费——这一福利在发布会现场引发了最热烈的欢呼。但站在行业观察的视角，这一决定仍值得深究，在重度SLG普遍依赖高ARPPU回收成本的既定思路上，投入了5亿元的《三王》，究竟凭什么敢送出“终身免费月卡”？
这背后或许一笔极其清醒的商业账与长线生态账。
从产品留存逻辑来看，终身免费月卡瞄准的不是短期噱头，而是SLG最稀缺的长线留存。每日80黄金配合游戏内388黄金五连抽的定价，相当于赋予了每位零氪及微氪玩家稳定且可预期的抽卡资源。对于一款重度沙盘游戏而言，平民与中小R玩家从来不是陪衬，而是构成同盟生态与千人战场活跃度的基石。
如果说终身免费月卡是拉高留存下限的保障，那么《三王》在卡池规则与养成机制上的改革，则是把“降价”真正融入了核心玩法循环：
首先是跨赛季的不重复橙卡招募池。《三王》设立了一套独立的不重复卡池机制，玩家在该池内抽到的橙色武将与战法会自动剔除，绝不重复产出。更关键的是，该卡池不仅保持与普通池一致的定价（388黄金五连、20抽保底），其抽取进度还会跨赛季继承。
其次是开创性的主公系统。“玩家自建武将”并非新鲜概念，但在《三王》这里却玩出了关键的战术价值，它将玩家自身扮演的主公打造成了一张可自由定制的万能核心卡，玩家不仅能通过日常游历免费将主公培养至满红、实现跨赛季属性保留，还能借助“拜师系统”结识各路名将并直接习得其自带战法。阵容缺输出便往输出方向专精，缺辅助便随时切换辅助定位，有力解决了SLG配队中最折磨人的“二缺一”困境。
还有支持装备自由买卖的交易行，普通玩家打野锻造出的极品装备可上架换取黄金，继而反哺抽卡与养成，形成了一套自给自足的内部经济循环。
叠加公测开局送出的双橙将与S1赛季最高18888黄金、220抽的丰厚投放，《三王》将“为玩家谋福利”落到了实处。
客观而言，降低抽卡门槛并不意味着一劳永逸地解决了重度SLG的商业化难题。但至少从产品设计逻辑上看，《三王》正在跳出传统SLG单纯压榨单用户付费深度的旧路径，转而尝试通过改善体验、做大活跃用户底盘，再依托长线赛季生态去沉淀商业回报。
生态破局
中重度SLG向来有个核心要素：人。
剥开配将、剧本、沙盘这些游戏内容，真正将游戏设计盘活的，是玩家的自主性，是由玩家自发编织的关系网，他们让每一次决策都有了分量，将每个赛季的较量演绎变成了一部由千万玩家共同书写、不可复刻的战场风云史。
在这方面，《三王》占据了宝贵先机。
目前，全国便已有超过1000家成熟顶尖强盟提前入驻备战，品鉴会现场，项目组更是专门设置了高规格的授旗仪式，麒麟龙吟、诸神黄昏、洛都赋、烬川等数十家同盟代表齐聚一堂。
《三王》能聚拢如此规模的头部同盟力量，离不开项目组前置的“听劝”诚意，早在三测开启前，B站发行团队便携手《三王》项目组跑遍全国多座重点城市，举办线下巡回意见倾听会与共创试玩会，将收集到的近千条核心玩家建议落实到了测试版本。
在赢得首批同盟信任的基础上，B站进一步围绕玩家组织、创作构建起了一套长线生态打法：
B站宣布首年投入不低于1亿元现金激励，并联合抖音与B站双端提供超1亿元价值的流量资源，启动创作者扶持计划。
B站恰好拥有放大这类玩家自叙事的最佳土壤。B站作为国内传统文化与游戏内容的核心社区，三国题材相关内容遍布B站历史考据、影视二创乃至鬼畜分区，当《三王》的战场与玩家持续碰撞出战场变量时，创作者便有了取之不尽的创作素材，届时再甫以高额现金与双端流量，迅速撬动“战局产生故事—UP主拆解传播—吸引泛三国受众入局”的生态自循环。
在玩家组织侧，B站也有了新策略，过往多数SLG在赛季结算后，同盟数据清零、成员各奔东西，社交关系极其脆弱，《三王》直接推出了同盟博物馆，通过官方层面的归档，把同盟在各个赛季的征战历程与荣耀时刻沉淀为可追溯的数字史诗。
除了搭建创作者与同盟这两大内部生态底座，《三王》也在外部打响了名号——10月初，《三王》正式接受第21届玄奘之路商学院戈壁挑战赛（简称“戈21”）组委会邀请，成为本届赛事唯一游戏合作伙伴。
作为国内极具影响力的商学院耐力赛事，戈赛每年汇聚逾5000名全球商学院EMBA、MBA学员及企业管理者，戈壁远征所考验的长线规划、资源调度与团队协同，与重度SLG的沙盘博弈在底层逻辑上高度同频。能够获得组委会主动邀约、与这群在现实商业世界里习惯了排兵布阵的决策者并肩同行，本身就是对《三王》谋略深度的有力背书。
千盟同聚，戈赛合作伙伴，段奕宏出任品牌代言人……《三王》在开服前便已攒下了扎实的人气值，而后续的内容激励与社交资产沉淀，则为游戏的长线运营增添了足够的底气，其开服后的生态表现无疑值得行业期待。
结语
老实说，眼下这个时间点，《三王》展现出的劲头，在行业里是相当罕见的。
大盘增长见顶、老牌头部产品凭借多年沉淀的社交关系牢牢守住基本盘，像《三王》这样肯下重本、直接从底层交战机制到商业化规则进行全面重构的重量级选手，确实已经许久未见了。
或许也正因如此，它也让行业久违地看到那种SLG玩家跃跃欲试的兴奋感。无论是大地图上纵横捭阖的沙盘博弈，还是微观战场里见招拆招的空间推演，《三王》的三维战场与机制创新，或许能让这群身经百战的玩家再度找回SLG的纯粹乐趣。
当然，在壁垒森严的SLG市场里，任何一款重度SLG想要真正搅动格局，最终都得靠漫长的赛季周期说话。《三王》究竟能释放出多大的能量，就让我们静候佳音吧。

news.title: European Game Worker unions publish manifesto warning against unchecked AI usage
news.summary_raw: Members in Ireland, Spain, and Milan have come together to outline concerns, grievances, pitfalls, and proposed solutions surrounding Generative AI use.

members.title: European Game Worker unions publish manifesto warning against unchecked AI usage
IWGB Game Workers Union leads manifesto on generative AI use in the industry

news.body:
European Game Worker unions publish manifesto warning against unchecked AI usage
Members in Ireland, Spain, and Milan have come together to outline concerns, grievances, pitfalls, and proposed solutions surrounding Generative AI use.
The IWGB Game Workers' Branch has released a joint proclamation with members from Game Workers Unite Ireland, CSVI of Spain, and FIOM-CGIL Milan Work Council to outline grievances and pitfalls with generative AI use (stylized in the publication as genAI) and proposed solutions for game developer unions to avoid using it.
The manifesto itself tackles the subject of genAI from several different angles, including socioeconomic and environmental, ethical, and concerns about production qualtiy.
The document's key argument, and one easy to imagine a worker's union focusing on, is that genAI creates worse working conditions and job losses. The published work asserts that genAI is being sold as an alternative to human workers, that its use creates unrealistic pressure in terms of policy and timescales, and that it enables employers to abdicate responsibility in both cases.
"GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce. Left unchecked, this harm will continue to grow and impact more workers, more games, and more players, even more acutely," the manifesto reads. "Our goal is to bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce, as well as to set guidelines and standards for games industry workers, stakeholders, and regulators, suggesting actions which can be taken to reduce—and ideally eliminate—these dangers."
The proclamation goes on to propose actions to reduce harm, including stopping all genAI use whenever possible. This year's State of the Game Industry survey states that 40 percent of game industry professionals use generative AI tools as part of their job, up from 36 percent the previous year. However, 55 percent say generative AI is having a negative impact on the industry, with 35 percent believing it is mixed, and only 8 percent arguing it is positive.
The manifesto has critics, as well. In a thread on the subject on Reddit's Gamedev community, one commenter points out that it is overly-focused on genAI as a threat to artists, but says little about it costing programming jobs.
At the bottom of the manifesto, a rather pointed frequently-asked-questions section posits why the collective game workers are "against the future."
"We are not [against the future]," the manifesto answers itself. "We simply believe that workers have the right to shape their future. Being exploited and overworked is not a future we are willing to accept. Time will prove genAI 'tools' and their usefulness, let us not be trampled in the meantime. The future is not yet written."

news.title: Xbox's Project Helix "is not a PC that can also play console games"
news.summary_raw: Xbox VP of Next Generation Jason Ronald has clarified that Project Helix is "designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games, not a PC that can also play console games."

members.title: Xbox's Project Helix "is not a PC that can also play console games"
Xbox teases Project Helix as 'a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC'

news.body:
Xbox's Project Helix "is not a PC that can also play console games"
Next Xbox console is "designed to be the ultimate gaming machine" by removing the "arbitrary constraints between console and PC games"
Xbox VP of Next Generation Jason Ronald has clarified that Project Helix is "designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games, not a PC that can also play console games."
In the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, Ronald described Project Helix as "the ultimate gaming machine – one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed."
"The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customisability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed Project Helix's console and PC compatibility in March, adding that the console will "lead in performance" for Xbox and PC games.
As Ronald previously discussed at GDC Festival of Gaming, Project Helix will utilise neural rendering, which uses AI models to enhance graphics. Ronald identified neural rendering as a particular focus for Project Helix, as it also addresses the ongoing component crisis.
"It's definitely a challenging time, but as a system and platform designer, it's one of the most exciting times, because we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also [making] things accessible and affordable."
"This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower [and] additional memory."
He concluded: "I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last ten years."
Reports last month indicated that Project Helix is expected to launch during the 2028 holiday season, with a projected price between $1,200 and $1,800.

members.title: 《NBA 2K27》与GTA联动！罪恶城版正式公布，这就是最好的一代NBA2K！
《NBA 2K27》×《GTA 6》联动宣传视频公开

news.body:
【2026年11月17日】 今日，2K正式宣布与Rockstar Games达成一项前所未有的史诗级合作——将《GTA》系列中标志性的“罪恶城”独特氛围全面引入《NBA 2K27》。由Visual Concepts开发、2K发行的这款年度篮球大作，将借此机会迎来史上规模最大的赛季联动。同时，官方正式发布了由迈阿密热火巨星巴姆·阿德巴约担纲封面的《NBA 2K27 罪恶城版》，并宣布第三赛季将于北京时间11月28日0:00正式上线。
NBA2K27作为近年来最好的一代NBA2K游戏，在玩家社区口碑迎来不小的翻盘，不仅带来了惊艳的跨界联动，更在底层动作引擎、核心玩法与画质表现上实现了全面升级，旨在为玩家呈现最真实、最沉浸的次世代篮球体验。
动作与画质双重革命：ProPLAY与DLSS 5加持
本作在Gameplay层面迎来了质的飞跃。依托全新的ProPLAY技术，游戏直接从真实的NBA比赛录像中提取并生成了超过7000+的全新动作，让球员的跑位、运球、对抗和投篮变得无比真实，完美还原了真实的NBA赛场感，从动作到玩法都堪称近年来的最佳之作。
在视觉表现上，PC端正式支持DLSS 5技术，结合极致的画面优化，光影、汗水与球场细节达到了以假乱真的地步，真正做到了“分不清现实与游戏”。此外，MyNBA与梦幻球队（MT）模式也迎来了深度优化，新增了丰富的罪恶城主题卡牌与限时玩法，进一步提升了策略与收集的乐趣。
MyCAREER沉浸升级：跨越时代的赛场体验
在备受瞩目的MyCAREER（MC）模式中，玩家将体验到前所未有的沉浸感。全新的Eras（世代）模式允许玩家选择不同的时代背景开启职业生涯，沉浸式体验与各个时代自己最喜欢的传奇球星同场竞技的梦想。无论是打破乔丹的统治，还是和魔鸟对抗成为三足鼎立亦或是和詹姆斯成为队友一起冲击克利夫兰的复兴，都能让纯正的篮球迷热血沸腾！
罪恶城接管第三赛季：文化与球场的完美融合
那个游戏和NBA2K27的史诗联动这次也引起了大家的关注，在为期七周的加长版第三赛季（北京时间2026年11月28日至2027年1月16日）中，罪恶城的霓虹光影将全面接管游戏。篮球之城的核心区域将替换为全新的“罪恶城风格公园”，包含海滨球场、霓虹粉彩酒店、鳄鱼麦加雕像以及街道上的超级跑车。NBA球馆也将替换为撒哈拉体育场。
玩家可以通过升级通行证解锁大量主题服饰，包括洛圣都球衣、吃得饱汉堡与当当钟员工服装，以及备受期待的Nike x Cactus Jack迈阿密热火球员版球衣。第三赛季还带来了多项特色活动：征服雷奥奈达、罪恶冲刺，以及每周三的“穿戴赚取”双倍声望活动。此外，梦幻球队模式也将迎来迈阿密热火的当红与传奇球星的罪恶城主题卡牌。
准备好迎接这场篮球与街头文化交织的狂欢了吗？让我们在罪恶城的霓虹下，制霸球场！

news.title: Unite Tokyo 2026 Keynote recap: Built for the speed of your ideas
news.summary_raw: Catch every highlight from the Unite Tokyo 2026 Keynote: Unity 7, ECS for All, Unity CLI, Synty Studios joining Unity, and the new Unity Fellowship.

members.title: Unite Tokyo 2026 Keynote recap: Built for the speed of your ideas

news.body:
Unite Tokyo 2026 Keynote recap: Built for the speed of your ideas
Adam Smith - Unity Technologies
Unite Tokyo 2026 had one idea at its center: Unity 7 is built for the speed of your ideas.
The Keynote showed this through three main themes. The first is how the Unity Engine enables great performance on every device, with ECS for All bringing greater compatibility between GameObjects and Entities, and scalable graphics built into the Engine by default. The second theme is faster creation, with Unity CLI available in 1.0 today, official plug-ins for coding agents, and a new Asset Library plug-in that searches the Unity Asset Store from inside the Editor. Finally, Unite Tokyo highlighted support for creators, with the announcement that Synty Studios is joining Unity. Two local studios, QualiArts and TVT, came onstage to share how they built their hit games hololive Dreams and Ratatan using Unity tools. The show closed with a look at the new Unity Fellowship, which will give ten indie teams each year resources, support, and $50,000 in cash to help finish up their games, with no revenue share and no recoup.
The bilingual show at Shibuya Bellesalle Gardens in Tokyo featured speakers in both Japanese and English, with content dubbed in for both audiences in livestreams. You can watch the entire show here, or read on for highlights, and stay tuned for English-language videos.
Welcome
We kicked things off with a sizzle reel showcasing amazing Made with Unity games from Japan. Masaru Agarida, Managing Director of Unity Japan, welcomed the audience to the first Unite since 2019.
I took to the stage next, reflecting on the history of Unity and where we came from and how the present moment in many ways brings us full circle. After all, Unity began with three developers in Copenhagen – Dave, Joachim, and Nicholas – who were building a game called GooBall and ended up turning their in-house tools into Unity 1.0, over 20 years ago. Their story reminds me that building a game is still hard, and success today comes from clarity of vision and speed of iteration. Unity 7 answers with faster performance across devices and faster creation, including official plug-ins for Claude, Codex, Google Antigravity, and Grok. Those plug-ins ship with skills Unity's own team built, reviewed, and security checked, and millions of Unity developers are already accelerating progress using the Unity CLI.
Graphics and performance across devices
Sangbae Nam from the engineering team covered the technical foundation. With ECS for All, every GameObject also becomes an Entity, so existing projects gain performance as engine systems move to the Entity Component System (ECS). In a demo with 5,000 spaceships, the GameObject version slowed as the count grew, while the ECS version held a steady frame rate. Unity 7.0 will also let you view and edit Entity data in the Inspector. You can check out the demo in English here.
On the graphics side, a new sample scene called Atrio showed URP's Surface Cache GI, a dynamic global illumination system that needs no lightmaps or baking. It ran at full resolution and 60 fps and is available on the Unity Asset Store today.
Unity Neural is a set of AI-powered tools for faster rendering and lower memory use. Neural Texture Compression cut Atrio's texture memory by nearly 30%. It arrives as an experimental feature in Unity 6.7 LTS, with a full release planned for Unity 7. Unity Graphics Kernel (UGK), a new graphics backend built on DirectX 12, Vulkan, and Metal, raised GPU performance in Atrio by more than 62% with ray tracing enabled.
Unity 6.7 LTS also brings customizable 2D graphics, Physics Core 2D authoring components, and a new 2D profiler, with a Bunny Blitz physics puzzle sample on the Unity Asset Store today.
Meta VR Glasses
Unity welcomed Chris Pruett of Meta, who talked about the Meta VR Glasses announced at Connect in September and Meta’s new developer tools that allow Unity developers to take advantage of this exciting new platform.
Meta VR Glasses are fully immersive virtual reality glasses, not augmented reality, weighing about 100 grams with no strap, micro-OLED displays, and compute in a separate puck. Players control them with their hands and eyes, and they run existing Quest apps on the same OS, SDKs, and store. Developers can build for them today on Unity 6.7 or newer with the v209 SDK. Meta VR Glasses ship next spring, and the developer tools are available now.
Unity CLI and Pipeline API
Next, Keijiro Takahashi walked through one project from first idea to team production and how Unity tools help to streamline that process. He started in the terminal, prompting an agent (Claude Code with Unity's official plug-in) to build a first-person puzzle prototype in a real Unity project. The agent wrote code, compiled, read errors, and playtested. Unity CLI is generally available today, and you can add your own commands to it.
The Unity Pipeline APIs then brought the same project into the browser for a wider team. A producer invited collaborators, an artist swapped placeholder assets with a simple drag and drop, then checked the result in Scene Preview, and a tester pinned notes directly to objects that opened in the Editor for the developer. The Unity Pipeline API is in beta with signups open, and general availability is planned for 2027. You can watch the full demo here.
Unity Asset Store and Synty Studios
I returned to the stage to showcase a new Asset Library plug-in that’s going to make it much easier for you to find and use assets that fit the style of your project. Type what you need, and it finds that single asset across the Unity Asset Store and the assets you already own, then drops it into your scene ready to use. It also adapts assets made for the Built-in Render Pipeline to URP, and the same search works from the CLI with any agent. Materials, animations, and sounds are coming soon.
The bigger news: Synty Studios is joining the Unity family. Cofounders Andrew Stairs and Mike Clephane joined me onstage to celebrate, sharing their vision that building games should be as much fun as playing them. Moving closer to Unity means the Synty team can feed their expertise back into the Engine, making integrations tighter so that assets are even faster and easier to use. Synty assets are available through the Asset Store and can be accessed through the CLI, and they’ll be available through Unity Spark from day one.
More support for creators with the Unity Fellowship
Aurore Dimopoulos announced the Unity Fellowship, an annual program for 10 indie teams roughly a year from launch. Each team receives a Unity point of contact, regular expert office hours, industry connections including publisher introductions, a presence at Unity events, PR and marketing support, and $50,000 in cash. There's no revenue share, no recoup, and teams keep their IP and creative control. Applications are open now, and the first Unity Fellowship studios will be announced at GDC in March 2027.
Watch the Keynote on YouTube.

EVE Vanguard、《神力科莎：拉力》(Assetto Corsa Rally) 等游戏支持 DLSS 4.5

news.body:
本周，EVE Vanguard 正式开启 7×24 全天 Alpha 测试，借助 DLSS 4.5 加速性能，增强图像质量。《神力科莎：拉力》(Assetto Corsa Rally)、Blender、《光年边疆》(Lightyear Frontier) 和《拆迁》(Teardown) 现也已支持 DLSS 4.5。
以下是最新和即将推出的 RTX 游戏详情：
● EVE Vanguard：Fenris Creations 打造的 EVE Vanguard 是一款以历史悠久的 《星战前夜》(EVE Online) 宇宙为背景的搜撤冒险 FPS。玩家将化身为凭借技术实现永生的战争克隆体，部署至危机四伏的行星地表，完成高风险任务、获取资源，并与其他玩家及敌对势力展开战斗；同时还可通过持续的成长系统在每一次部署中不断增强实力。游戏将于 2027 年在 Steam 上线，想抢先体验的玩家现可购买创始人礼包，通过 EVE 启动器参与 Alpha 测试。为提升 GeForce RTX 系统的性能与图像质量，首发版本即支持 DLSS 4.5，及超分辨率、多帧生成、DLAA 和 NVIDIA Reflex 等技术。
● 《神力科莎：拉力》(Assetto Corsa Rally)：505 Games 与 Supernova Games Studios 联合打造的《神力科莎：拉力》(Assetto Corsa Rally) 是一款为精准的操控与挑战而打造的高拟真拉力模拟游戏。《神力科莎：拉力》(Assetto Corsa Rally) 由 Kunos Simulazioni 提供技术合作支持，基于广受赞誉的 《神力科莎》(Assetto Corsa) 物理引擎，针对拉力赛的特定需求进行专项优化，采用定制版虚幻引擎 5 开发。《神力科莎：拉力》(Assetto Corsa Rally) 已于去年开启抢先体验，并支持具备多帧生成、帧生成和超分辨率技术的 DLSS 4。全套技术即将升级至 DLSS 4.5，以进一步提升图像质量、增强性能，并将新增动态多帧生成功能，持续优化每位车手的竞速体验。
● Blender 5.3：Blender 是一款免费开源软件，提供 3D 建模与渲染工具，广泛用于电视、电影等众多领域的内容与特效创作。全新发布的 Blender 5.3 新增支持 DLSS 4.5 光线重建视口降噪功能，让创作者在执行耗时的渲染任务之前，即可查看并编辑细节显著提升的作品，从而大幅改善迭代与开发体验并提高效率。Blender 5.3 原生支持 RTX Spark 设备，助力拥有新设备的用户更高效地完成创作与渲染，进一步优化使用体验。查看页面，了解 Blender 5.3 的全部新增功能。
● 《光年边疆》(Lightyear Frontier)：FRAME BREAK 打造的 《光年边疆》(Lightyear Frontier)开放世界机甲农场游戏。在星际间安家，经营自己的农场，制造机器，为困境中的边疆殖民地送去所需物资。经过 5 年的抢先体验开发，《光年边疆》(Lightyear Frontier)现已推出 1.0 更新，带来大量全新内容游戏的正式发布为 GeForce RTX 和 RTX Spark 玩家带来 DLSS 4.5 超分辨率与 DLAA 支持。现有集成功能同步升级，显著提升图像质量。
● 《拆迁》(Teardown)：在 Tuxedo Labs 打造的完全可破坏模拟体素世界中，策划一场完美劫案。《拆迁》(Teardown) 在玩家中“好评如潮”，一切都可以被破坏、移动，或被改造成一条捷径。玩家需要发挥创造性的解决问题能力、蛮力，以及利用周围的一切，开创出一条穿越关卡的高效路线。游戏近期更新新增对最新 DLSS 超分辨率模型的支持，可提升《拆迁》(Teardown)完全可破坏世界中的帧率。对于拥有高性能系统的的玩家可开启 DLAA大限度提升图像质量。

news.title: Creating Real-Time Desert Temple Environment In Unreal Engine 5
news.summary_raw: Marc Castells shared his approach to building a desert scene with a temple, discussing how he expanded on the original concept and found the right balance between realism and stylization.

members.title: Creating Real-Time Desert Temple Environment In Unreal Engine 5

news.body:
Creating Real-Time Desert Temple Environment In Unreal Engine 5
Marc Castells shared his approach to building a desert scene with a temple, discussing how he expanded on the original concept and found the right balance between realism and stylization.
Introduction
Hi! My name is Marc Castells, and I'm a 3D Environment Artist based in Barcelona, Spain. My professional career began in the animation industry, where I worked for two years at Icon Creative Studio in Vancouver on Star Wars: Young Jedi Adventures for Disney+.
After working in animation, I decided to move into video games. Kreaktivate was my introduction to real-time environment art, and I continued learning through mentorships with artists like Iñigo Cebollero. Later, I joined Think Tank Training Centre to further develop my skills. Desert Temple gave me the chance to bring these skills together in a single project.
Getting Started
I chose Edward Barons' Ball Temple concept because it offered a good balance between visual appeal, complexity, and production time.
The environment looks quite detailed, but most of the architecture is based on a main temple building repeated in the background with some variations. This allowed me to reuse assets and save time without losing visual interest. I also wanted to work on a more open environment, where I could practice creating landscapes, vegetation, and material blending. It was a good opportunity to improve these skills while building a complete scene in Unreal Engine 5.
Workflow
Expanding the original composition was a very organic process. As I started exploring different camera angles, I quickly noticed that there were many empty areas in the environment that weren't visible in the main shot.
To fill those spaces, I tried to follow the visual language of the original concept. For example, I continued the existing paths, vegetation areas, and architectural elements to make the environment feel consistent from different viewpoints.
Adding more detail doesn't always make an environment better. Too many elements can distract the viewer, so I wanted the temple to remain the focal point. The rocks, vegetation, and surrounding architecture had to support the composition, with enough quieter spaces for the eye to rest without making the environment feel empty.
Most of the architecture and interior props were modeled in Maya using a standard workflow. I reused elements such as windows and created variations of the main temple with Lattice and Soft Selection, which saved me from modeling every background building from scratch.
As mentioned earlier, most architectural assets were modeled in Maya. I created the vegetation in SpeedTree, where I could adjust the polygon count directly.
The rocks were the only assets I sculpted in ZBrush. I made a small kit of two large rocks, one rock wall, and three smaller variations for scattering. I blocked them out in Maya, sculpted details in ZBrush, and used Decimation to reduce the polygon count while preserving their shapes. Then I returned to Maya for UV unwrapping, baked the maps in Substance Painter, and set up the final material blending in Unreal Engine using RGB masks.
Texturing
To find a balance between realism and stylization, I mainly followed a PBR workflow, making sure the materials reacted to light in a physically believable way. I think the stylized look comes more from the original concept, the shapes of the architecture, and the color palette, with elements like the bright red flowers and turquoise water contrasting with the desert environment.
One of my main goals for this project was to practice RGB masking, a technique commonly used in video game environments. The idea is to store three different grayscale masks in the red, green, and blue channels of a single texture. I created these masks in Substance 3D Painter and exported them as one RGB texture.
Then, in Unreal Engine, I used those masks to blend different materials together. For example, the water stains and streaks on the temple walls were created using masks painted in Substance 3D Painter, which controlled where the different surface materials appeared. I used the same workflow for the metal roofs, blending the copper surface with patina to create an aged, weathered look. This allowed me to control the material transitions while keeping the workflow flexible and relatively efficient.
I experimented with two ways of blending assets with the environment. I used Runtime Virtual Texturing to help the rocks pick up colors and texture variation from the landscape, softening the transition between them and the ground. I also created an occlusion-based material function to add dirt near the base of objects, with a controllable fade height. Both techniques helped make assets feel more connected to their surroundings, and I wanted to explore how each approach worked.
Throughout the project, I received weekly feedback from Sergei Panin, my mentor at Think Tank Training Centre, who helped me improve the overall quality of the environment. I also worked closely with Iñigo Cebollero, who had been mentoring me outside Think Tank, particularly in Substance Designer and material creation. He helped me better understand how materials should behave and how to make them look more believable.
Composition
I think it's important to remember that a concept is a visual guide, not something that always needs to be followed exactly. Sometimes, small changes are necessary to make the environment work better in 3D.
For example, if you compare the original concept with my final render, you'll notice that the main temple is positioned at a slightly different distance from the camera. To my eye, the foreground and background in the artwork almost seemed to use different fields of view. My first step was to find an FOV that worked well for the entire scene, keeping the main temple as the focal point without making the background feel too distant.
Once I was happy with the camera, I started the blockout using very simple shapes. At this stage, I focused mainly on the overall landscape, the position of the main temple, the shape of the river in the foreground, and the mountains in the background. I didn't worry too much about vegetation or small details at first. Those elements came later, as the environment gradually developed and the main composition started to work.
For the mountains, I manually combined, rotated, and reused my two main rock assets to create larger formations that matched the original concept as closely as possible. For the vegetation and smaller rocks, I used Unreal Engine's Foliage Mode. Rather than scattering everything evenly, I adjusted the density to create natural-looking clusters and leave some open spaces.
Lighting & Rendering
My lighting setup was actually quite simple. I used a Directional Light, Skylight, Sky Atmosphere, and Exponential Height Fog to create atmospheric depth and make the distant mountains look slightly faded.
I also used an HDRI Backdrop, but only for the sky background, without affecting the scene's lighting. I downloaded a sky image and edited it in Photoshop to adjust the position of the clouds and make them fit the composition better.
For the lighting itself, I wanted to achieve a bright midday atmosphere. The main challenge was finding the right balance between the Directional Light and the Skylight to get enough contrast without making the shadows too dark.
I think shadows play a very important role in this environment, especially in the main shot. The large shadow covering the right side of the foreground helps frame the scene and directs the viewer's attention towards the main temple. I also used shadows at the base of the mountains and behind the background buildings to separate the different layers of the scene and give the composition more depth.
For the atmosphere, I combined two different effects. The Exponential Height Fog created the general haze and depth, while a simple Niagara particle system added some moving dust in the background, making the environment feel a little more alive.
Finally, I rendered the scene using Unreal Engine's Movie Render Queue and made a few adjustments in DaVinci Resolve. My main goal was to keep the shots visually consistent rather than heavily alter the original renders.
Conclusion
One of the biggest challenges for me was going beyond the original concept. In my previous projects, I hadn't really needed to develop areas that weren't shown in the artwork, so filling those empty spaces while keeping everything visually consistent was something new for me.
Since real-time environment art is still relatively new to me, this project has been a huge learning experience. Almost every stage brought something new to learn and apply. Sometimes, even towards the end of production, I discovered better techniques or started noticing things that weren't working as well as I thought, so I went back to improve them.
For beginners, my first piece of advice would be to choose projects carefully. It's easy to browse ArtStation, find an amazing concept, and want to recreate it in 3D. But it's important to understand your current skills and how much work you can realistically complete in the time you have. A smaller, well-executed project is often better than an overly ambitious one.
My second piece of advice would be to never be afraid of asking for feedback. We've all been beginners, and sometimes it's difficult to see what's wrong with our own work. Sharing your progress and receiving constructive criticism is one of the best ways to improve. There are many great communities on Discord, Reddit, and other platforms where artists are happy to help each other.
Don't be afraid to show your work, even if it's not perfect. That's part of the learning process.

news.title: How BeamNG.drive Brought Its Soft-Body Physics to PS5
news.summary_raw: The BeamNG team discusses keeping BeamNG.drive's soft-body physics unchanged on PS5, explains how they optimized memory and performance for the console, and talks about rebuilding the UI and controls for gamepad players.

members.title: How BeamNG.drive Brought Its Soft-Body Physics to PS5

news.body:
How BeamNG.drive Brought Its Soft-Body Physics to PS5
The BeamNG team discusses keeping BeamNG.drive's soft-body physics unchanged on PS5, explains how they optimized memory and performance for the console, and talks about rebuilding the UI and controls for gamepad players.
BeamNG.drive has been popular on PC for years because of its soft-body physics, open-ended sandbox structure, and endlessly shareable crashes. When bringing the game to PS5, what parts of that core identity did the team know had to remain untouched?
First and foremost, the physics. It's at the heart of BeamNG's identity, the core of what makes BeamNG, well, BeamNG. The PS5 version runs the same soft-body simulation as the PC version. That was non-negotiable for two reasons. First, physics is the core of nearly everything we do, so keeping it identical guarantees that a vehicle built and tuned for PC behaves the same way on PS5. And second, the more of that foundation the two platforms can share, the less effort goes into improving and maintaining both versions.
Just as important was the freedom to do whatever you want with it. Whether you're racing, exploring, or just seeing what happens when you drive something off a cliff, that freedom to experiment had to remain intact. We didn't want the console version to feel like a different game, or a simplified version of the PC experience.
The game has become incredibly viral on YouTube, TikTok, and other platforms because players can stage crashes, experiments, stunts, police chases, obstacle courses, and strange vehicle scenarios. Why do you think BeamNG.drive works so well as a creator-driven spectacle?
Because the results are unpredictable. Even we don't always know what's going to happen when you put something together and press Play. Every impact is calculated in the moment rather than played back, so no two runs turn out quite the same. A creator can start with the simplest idea, like driving a bus down a ridiculous hill, and the physics does the rest. You don't need scripted moments when the simulation can create something entertaining on its own.
That ties back to a higher-level goal of ours: to simulate reality. The better we do at that, the more people can effectively direct their own movies inside the simulated world, deciding the scenario and letting the physics supply the payoff. Some of those people are highly talented, and the results are worth watching.
A lot of people discover BeamNG through those videos, and plenty of them end up making videos of their own – which keeps the cycle going.
BeamNG's soft-body physics engine is the foundation of the experience, with vehicles built from structures that can bend, deform, and break in ways that feel unusually physical. How do you explain that technology to players who may be discovering the game for the first time on console?
Most driving games simulate how a vehicle moves. BeamNG also simulates how the vehicle behaves as a physical structure. Every vehicle has a skeleton of masses connected by springs, and the car you see follows that skeleton. When you hit something, we're not swapping in a damaged model or playing an animation – the forces travel through the structure, and whatever takes too much load bends, breaks, or comes off. The same structure drives handling and suspension, which is why adding weight, even a passenger, changes how a vehicle drives.
Underneath that is a passion for physics at every level: conserving the basic properties that the real universe conserves, like energy, momentum, and mass; being deliberate about how cars, trucks, and objects are actually constructed; and finally making the whole thing feel right to a driver holding the wheel – plus obsessing over the smallest details, which are often the coolest ones. The best explanation, though, is still to pick a car and drive it into a wall.
From a technical standpoint, what were the biggest challenges in bringing BeamNG.drive's physics simulation to PS5, especially around CPU load, vehicle deformation, collision complexity, AI traffic, large maps, and maintaining responsiveness?
BeamNG does an enormous amount of work behind the scenes, and much of it happens at the same time. Every vehicle is its own physical simulation, and when you add traffic, collisions, and large environments, that complexity grows quickly. Our custom engine has always been heavily tailored to prioritize physics over any other subsystem, so the goal on PS5 was never simply to make it run – it was feature parity with the other platforms, retaining identical physics behavior and identical vehicle structures, while preserving the responsiveness players expect, all inside a fixed hardware budget.
That came in stages. First, making it fit: a lot of work went into optimizing memory use and reducing install size, and reducing the memory footprint matters just as much as raw speed, because it determines how many vehicles you can have on screen before the hardware runs out of headroom. Then, making it fast: physics is one of the biggest CPU users in the game, so heavy optimization happened there and on the GPU/rendering side – and since headroom is useful no matter where it comes from, it was pursued across every subsystem, not just the physics engine. Lastly, making it robust: a change set that large created a lot of bugs, and a great deal of time went into hunting them down.
We also made the whole thing an even bigger challenge by pushing for split-screen at the same time, which multiplies the computational demand on both physics and rendering.
There were two practical results of all this. The vast majority of the optimizations are cross-platform, so they benefit Windows, Linux, Steam Deck, and Arm alongside PS5. And the quality presets for PS5 and PS5 Pro were chosen carefully. That is not a simple task when the simulation can be used in wildly different ways. Finding a configuration that serves all gameplay styles is key to keeping the framerate high in the most common scenarios.
A lot of the appeal comes from the fact that crashes are not canned animations; they emerge from the simulation. How does that affect vehicle art, modeling, rigging, materials, damage states, and the way vehicles need to be constructed compared with a more traditional racing game?
Our vehicles have to behave convincingly, not just look convincing. You can't just build a beautiful car and then add a few damage effects at the end – for something to behave correctly, it needs to be constructed correctly too, because the physics has to understand how that vehicle should respond when things go wrong.
That changes how a vehicle is built from the ground up. In a traditional racing game, an artist models the car and a few damaged versions of it. For us, the visual mesh sits on top of the physics skeleton and has to deform with it at any point, in any direction. Every detail also costs performance, so it's always a balance.
That's why vehicle creation is one of the most complicated things we do. A single vehicle involves 3D meshes, physics skeletons, audio, and control software for systems like ABS and ESC, so our designers, engineers, and programmers all have to work together to produce the visuals, the physics, and the higher-level mechanisms. Some vehicles need specialized simulation on top of that – heavy machinery, for example, comes with hydraulics and its own control systems.
BeamNG.drive is not only a crash simulator; it also supports racing, crawling, delivery missions, police chases, scenarios, free roam, and experimentation. What do you think about designing content for a game where players often create their own goals?
We want to give players things to do without telling them what they should be doing. Missions, races, deliveries, and other activities provide structure, but the sandbox itself is where players discover what uniquely interests them. We think of it as offering opportunities rather than obligations.
Maps aren't built around a single route, and vehicles come with swappable parts, so players can build something close to a factory spec or something no factory would ever approve. If someone starts a delivery mission and ends up spending an hour exploring a mountain road instead, that's not a design failure; that's the game working as intended.
What did the team learn from the PC community, modders, and content creators about what players actually do in BeamNG.drive once they get their hands on the sandbox?
That players will always find uses for your game you never imagined. We've seen BeamNG turned into everything from a serious driving simulator to an elaborate physics playground.
The modding community in particular has shown just how far the game can be pushed. One of the most consistent lessons we've learned through the years is that you don't always need to dictate how your game should be played. Sometimes your job is simply to give people the tools and let them surprise you.
For the PS5 version, how did you approach controls, UI, onboarding, camera behavior, and player guidance for an audience that may not have the same expectations as longtime PC simulation players?

news.summary_raw: The Grammys are celebrating a suite of stellar video game soundtracks—but one indie dev says the academy rejected their score for being heavy on vocals.

members.title: This year's video game Grammy nominations reveal Academy's potential favor against songs with vocals

news.body:
The 2023 Grammy award nominations have been released, celebrating a fine batch of high-quality video game soundtracks. But in an interesting twist, information from an indie developer has offered insights on what the Recording Academy is looking to honor for its relatively new interactive category (the award was spun up in 2023).
Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora – From the Ashes (John Paesano)
007: First Light (Joe Henson & Alexis Leon Smith)
Ghost of Yōtei (Toma Otowa)
Marvel’s Wolverine (David Fleming)
Star Wars: Zero Company (Gordy Haab)
Previous winners for this award include Austin Wintory for Sword of the Sea, Winifred Phillips for Wizardy: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord, Stephen Barton and Gordy Haab for Star Wars: Jedi Survivor, and Stephanie Economou for Assassin's Creed: Valhalla.
One thing you may notice is that neither the nominations list nor the winners list include soundtracks that focus heavily on standout vocal songs. It turns out this may be by design, as Unbeatable writer and director RJ Lake commented on social media site Bluesky that the game's mostly-vocal soundtrack was not a good fit for the category as envisioned. Lake says that D-Cell received a response from the Grammys after submitting a consideration form stating that vocal songs are not what the voting judges are looking for in this category, leaving D-Cell in a bit of a lurch. It was seemingly not issued as a hard and steadfast rule, but rather practical knowledge of what the nominating body expects from the category.
"[For the record] we probably wouldn't have gotten nominated anyway (in many ways likely too indie and too nontraditional regardless) but it blew my mind when we got an email about the grammy submission FROM the grammy awards saying vocal songs weren't supposed to be considered for game soundtrack nominations," Lake wrote. "They told us so we could mold our submission to that. it's not a strict rule anywhere in the awards description, but from what we were told the voting body does Not Go For It and that's more than a little baffling when your game is basically made out of vocal songs originally written for the game."
It is a bit surprising that the Grammy for video games and interactive media seems to mostly dismiss anything beyond instrumental music, but Lake's experience seems to match up with the list of nominees since the categories' inception. Though one of the nominees this year, 007 First Light, does feature a prominent Lana Del Rey song as part of the game's opening, but it's unclear if the voting judges are nominating the soundtrack despite that.
The 69th Annual Grammy Awards are scheduled to take place on Sunday, February 7, 2027, though the video game soundtrack award is presented at the premiere show a few hours before the televised broadcast.

members.title: Meet the company that finds Chinese game developers to work on Western IP

news.body:
Meet the company that finds Chinese game developers to work on Western IP
Yodo1 has just announced a deal to bring AMC's The Walking Dead to China – co-CEO Henry Fong explains the firm's strategy
Earlier this month, Yodo1 Games announced a strategic digital licensing partnership with the American firm AMC Global Media, which is behind television series such as The Walking Dead and Anne Rice's Interview with the Vampire. Yodo1 is tasked with finding and supporting Chinese game developers and publishers in order to create video games based on AMC's franchises.
There has been much talk in recent years of how Chinese games are starting to make huge inroads into the North American and European markets, through blockbuster titles like Genshin Impact. But the opportunity also goes the other way: Human: Fall Flat, for example, which has now reached 60 million players, owes a large part of its success to its popularity in China..
Yodo1 has already worked with big Western firms like Hasbro and Netflix, and the firm's co-founder and co-CEO, Henry Fong, talked to GamesIndustry.biz about the latest deal with AMC, the challenges of translating IP for Chinese audiences, and why firms should consider licensing their IP.
Can you tell me more about Yodo1? How did it start, and where are you based?
Yodo1 was founded in Beijing in 2011 primarily as a mobile game publisher. Over time, we recognised a greater opportunity to connect China's domestic gaming industry with global entertainment brands. This grew to the point that in 2019, we began developing our Brands in Games business, focused on bringing established IP into games through licensing partnerships, collaborations, and original game development. Today, we work with major entertainment companies, including Hasbro, Netflix, AMC Networks, Paramount, and others.
Although our roots are in China, we're now a fully remote, global company, with team members across Asia, Europe, and the Americas. That international presence is particularly important because we are working across very different markets, business cultures and licensing environments.
What kinds of companies are you approaching about licensing IP?
We work with a broad range of IP owners, but we primarily focus on entertainment brands, which means film and television studios, animation companies, gaming publishers, toy companies, and other major consumer brands.
Our partnerships cover different business models. Sometimes we're bringing an entertainment franchise into an existing successful mobile game through a limited-time collaboration. Other times, we're exploring standalone games built entirely around a particular IP.
It's important to say that our involvement is much deeper than simply acting as a conduit between licensee and licensor. Our key value is our experience in both the Chinese and Western markets and our ability to bring together the best aspects of both. So for every project, we want to develop a deeper understanding of a franchise's priorities, upcoming releases, target audiences and long-term ambitions. This allows us to proactively identify the right gaming opportunities, whether that's a limited-time collaboration, a new game, or a broader partnership involving multiple developers.
What challenges have you faced when it comes to The Walking Dead and Interview with the Vampire? Are Chinese developers familiar with these franchises? Has there been a steep learning curve?
The Walking Dead actually has a big fanbase in China, which has grown ever since the streaming platform Youku launched it in 2012. In fact, I think it was the most-watched show on the whole platform. Plus, its themes of survival, zombies, post-apocalyptic environments, and human conflict translate naturally into genres that are already extremely popular among Chinese developers, particularly strategy and survival games. We've seen this through previous collaborations, including Puzzles & Survival and Last Shelter: Survival.
Chinese consumers aren't already familiar with Interview with the Vampire, but that gives us an opportunity to bring something fresh and new to gamers. It's a sophisticated franchise with rich storytelling, complex characters, and a very specific aesthetic, so it's about explaining what makes Interview with the Vampire distinctive, from its character relationships and gothic atmosphere to the emotional depth of its storytelling. So while they may not know this specific IP, the universal themes within it are what gamers love.
Another important aspect of what Yodo1 brings to our relationship with IP holders is the work we do to keep franchises top of mind within the Chinese developer ecosystem, regardless of whether a particular brand is active within China. Many domestic developers operate games with large international audiences, so players are often interested in global entertainment franchises. That means there's an opportunity to keep developers engaged, informed, and excited about brands that may not necessarily have the same level of local visibility, but still have strong appeal among their global players.
One of the most important lessons is that brand recognition alone is not enough. Using a known IP is often seen as a shortcut to success, but we've learned that part of our role must be to translate the creative identity of the franchise into something developers can understand, execute, and monetise without losing what makes that IP special, and above all, to ensure the use of the IP feels authentic rather than forced.
Why should companies consider giving their IP to Chinese developers?
I think one of the biggest misconceptions is that licensing to a Chinese developer means you're only targeting the Chinese market. Yes, China has become a big market in its own right, but Chinese studios are behind many of the big global hits – especially on mobile, but now increasingly they are having global success on PC and console too.
To put the influence of Chinese game companies into context, according to Sensor Tower's December 2025 data, 33 of the world's top 100 mobile game publishers by revenue were Chinese companies, collectively accounting for approximately 34.6% of the revenue generated by those top 100 publishers. In 2025 alone, Chinese-developed games generated approximately US$20.5 billion in overseas revenue, with the United States, Japan, and South Korea among their largest international markets.
The other important point is that Chinese developers have developed substantial expertise in live operations, player engagement, monetisation, and running games over long periods. So for IP holders, it's not just about accessing China, but instead accessing some of the most commercially experienced game developers in the global market.
What kinds of IP would work in terms of being transferred to a Chinese development team? And what wouldn't work well?
It's less about what IP they can work with than about whether the IP fits the game's mechanics, audience, visual style, and commercial objectives. For example, action, science fiction, fantasy, horror, and survival franchises can translate very well into strategy, RPG, or survival games because they often feature recognisable characters, environments, weapons, and other elements that naturally integrate into gameplay. But we've also seen successful opportunities with lifestyle, fashion, and character-driven brands, particularly in casual, simulation, and merge games. A romantic drama franchise, for example, might not be an obvious match for a combat game, but it could work extremely well in a narrative-driven or makeover experience.
This is also where data and market intelligence become increasingly important. We've developed tools such as IPverse to bring a more structured, data-informed approach to IP licensing. By combining insights into entertainment franchises, game genres, developer profiles, and market opportunities with our team's industry expertise, we can make better-informed decisions about which brands and games have the strongest potential to work together.
Where things become more challenging is when the collaboration requires a significant change to the core identity of either the IP or the game. Some properties also depend heavily on specific actors, performances, music, or complex storytelling, which can introduce additional licensing and creative restrictions. So, to avoid these complications, we try to avoid situations where a brand is simply added to a game just because it's famous.
How are you accommodating China's censorship laws?
As you know, China has a very specific regulatory environment for games, so this is something that has to be considered early on in any licensing discussion. But equally, a game developed in China doesn't automatically mean that every collaboration will launch in China.
For games that will be published in mainland China, we need to assess local regulatory requirements, including content restrictions and game approvals, and make any necessary modifications. In some cases, you can have a game made for a global launch, with the China version having a few differences. Really, it's not all that different to some Western countries that have specific rules – we can always go back to the famous example of Carmageddon, where the German version needed to change all the NPCs to robots in order to get approval.
What kind of deal do you offer IP holders?
Because each collaboration is essentially unique, we don't believe in a one-size-fits-all licensing model. The commercial structure depends on the IP, the developer, the type of game, the length of the collaboration, and the territories involved – plus the scope and risks involved.
From our perspective, the most important thing is creating a commercially sustainable deal for both sides. A successful partnership needs to generate meaningful value for the IP holder while giving the developer enough flexibility and commercial incentive to create a strong experience for players. Idea

members.title: UK tribunal dismisses £2bn PlayStation class-action suit which alleged unfair pricing over 30% cut on PlayStation Store

news.body:
UK tribunal dismisses £2bn PlayStation class-action suit which alleged unfair pricing over 30% cut on PlayStation Store
Competition Appeal Tribunal finds that consumers have sufficient alternatives in the form of physical releases and rival consoles, unlike previous judgement against the App Store
A long-running class action lawsuit alleging that Sony was engaged in monopolistic behaviour and unfair price-fixing on PlayStation games has been dismissed by the UK competition authorities, following a trial earlier this year.
The case, which was brought in 2022 by consumer campaigner Alex Neill, alleged that Sony was engaged in exclusionary behaviour by creating a "closed ecosystem" that rendered digital users an "entirely captive class", enabling it to enact “excessive and unfair” charges on downloads from the PlayStation Store. It claimed that digital game content would have been approximately 20% cheaper if Sony's practices were not in place.
The claim covered 12.2 million users and said they were in line for a payment of £162 each, with a total cost of around £2 billion ($2.6 billion).
The claim was dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in a judgement issued today, which found that consumers had sufficient alternatives to Sony's digital store in the form of physical copies - which the firm recently announced would be discontinued - and alternative console platforms.
The tribunal also concluded that Sony's ecosystem had not been created as an open platform, and to make it capable of supporting third-party stores would require "significant cost and effort" that would likely result in reduced security and performance.
The judgement held that "there was strong evidence of a willingness of consumers to switch consoles following an increase in games prices," citing Sony research which "forecast commercial harm to Sony if it allowed PlayStation game prices to be uncompetitive with Xbox."
It said that the claim's assertion that players were trapped in a closed ecosystem was "not credible as it was based almost entirely on theoretical assumptions, which did not hold good in important respects in the real world. The contention that the competitive price would be 20% lower than the actual retail price was not made out."
The tribunal had previously found against Apple in a similar case in 2025, judging that the firm had abused its dominant position by forcing users through the App Store and its 30% commission rate. Apple has subsequently relaxed its policies to enable alternative web stores, which has driven a boom in third-party stores from providers like Xsolla and AppCharge.

ai.body:
17th November 2026 - Link Blog
External sandboxes for coding agents. I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.
I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.
My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.
To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:
- external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
- external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
- external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!
Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.
The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:
I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
17th November 2026
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I’ve released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it’s now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.
You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:
- Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script
- Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI
- Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository
- Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette
- Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools
The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.
As an example, consider the following URL:
Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you’ll find yourself on a page that looks like this:
That’s Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.
Let’s break down that URL to see what it’s doing:
https://lite.datasette.io/
?install=datasette-maplibre
&url=https://.../demo.db
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent
The ?install=datasette-maplibre
installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=...
as many times as you like to load more plugins.
&url=https://.../demo.db
loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers—I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent
is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette—here it’s loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries
SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23
is a URL-encoded #
) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent
column in the data.
That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year.
The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README.
I’ve already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here’s a recent issue describing a pagination bug—I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:
Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score—click next and the second page is empty.
Here’s that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score
How this works, using service workers
Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.
The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML
.
This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML
don’t execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.
The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.
Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io
domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:
/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)
Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/
prefix. What’s that about?
The /app/<session>/
prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.
Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre
plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.
The service worker for lite.datasette.io
is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.
Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.
(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)

Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite
I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite.
Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.
Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.
In the past I’ve used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it’s not a trivial process.
WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.
datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:
pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl
That’s for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.
Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite=
URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1
, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.
Once I’d built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool](https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. This should work for every other Python app, too
Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick—running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.
C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.
One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.
I’d love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.
